items.abstract: kALDo 2.3.0 adds a dedicated non-analytic correction engine, anharmonic free-energy corrections from the cumulant expansion, and memory checks for parallel force constants. It also rebuilds IFC interpolation, which changes some results, and fixes two bugs that affected force constants in 2.2.x. New features The non-analytic correction (NAC) has a dedicated engine that uses the Quantum ESPRESSO rigid-ion convention for q2r input and the phonopy (Gonze-Lee) convention otherwise. It turns on when the atoms carry a dielectric tensor and nonzero (n_atoms, 3, 3) Born charges. The new is_nac=False turns it off, and nac_q_direction sets the direction of approach to Gamma. Active NAC requires a diagonal supercell and rejects distance_threshold ( #307 ). kaldo.cumulant computes anharmonic free-energy corrections from the phonon cumulant expansion ( F1_from_fc , F2_from_fc , cumulant_thermo ) ( #283 ). Parallel force-constant calculations check available memory first. With n_workers=None , kALDo uses the smaller of the CPU count and the memory-safe limit (2.2.x used all CPUs); an explicit n_workers above the limit raises MemoryError . KALDO_MEMORY_HEADROOM sets the fraction of available memory kept free (default 0.05). The estimate covers host memory only, so pass GPU calculators as a factory ( #248 , #321 ). The documentation now covers installation with uv ( #300 ) and has user guides for IFC interpolation and the non-analytic correction ( #308 ). Changes that affect results IFC interpolation no longer depends on where the unit-cell origin is drawn ( #306 ). For systems periodic in all three directions, both the default is_unfolding=False and is_unfolding=True use the shortest Wigner-Seitz images of each atom pair; TDEP and QE d3q third-order data keep their own convention.…

items.abstract: At SC26, an annual supercomputing conference taking place this week in Chicago, NVIDIA is introducing the DGX Spark HPC Developer Kit for researchers, academics and developers. The kit is a four-node cluster of NVIDIA DGX Spark systems , each connected directly to its two neighbors in a ring, with an NVIDIA HPC SDK installation playbook coming soon. Researchers get a place at their desk to run multi-node scientific workloads, AI models and agents, instead of waiting for time on a shared GPU cluster. The kit puts the GB10 Grace Blackwell Superchip on researchers’ desks. A Supercomputing Lab on Any Desk The DGX Spark Developer Kit changes how researchers work. Read All NVIDIA Announcements From SC26 It scales from one system, or node, to four — linked directly to one another over NVIDIA ConnectX-7 networking, with no network switch to buy or set up. At four nodes, it provides 512GB of combined memory and 16TB of NVMe storage that provides researchers more capacity to distribute models and scientific workloads across the cluster. With NVFP4, researchers can deploy models with up to 700B parameters locally across the four DGX Spark clusters, such as DeepSeek V4.1. With that much power at the desk, researchers with a fixed compute and server allocation no longer have to wait in a queue for every job. Teams can develop and debug on their own, saving server hours for production runs and keeping unpublished results, and proprietary datasets on premises. The playbook for NVIDIA HPC SDK is coming soon, bringing GPU-accelerated C, C++ and Fortran compilers, libraries and message passing interface tools to the DGX Spark cluster — the same development tools used on NVIDIA-powered supercomputers. Teams can build and test scientific applications across four nodes, check how…
items.title: NVIDIA DGX Spark Developer Kit Turns a Desk Into a Supercomputing Lab

items.abstract: Quantum processor deployments at supercomputing centers have grown nearly sevenfold over the past five years, with nearly 30 supercomputing centers around the world now in the process of deploying over 50 quantum processors. Many of these centers use Slurm to run scientific supercomputing workloads, so expanding its support for quantum processors builds on familiar workflows and tools, enabling computational chemists, nuclear physicists and materials scientists to bring quantum computing into their research domains without friction. In a new release, Slurm builds on previous work with IBM, Pasqal and the wider quantum computing community to allow QPU builders to create a single interface to their hardware for every supercomputing center, through a simple file. This makes it easier than ever for HPC centers and QPU builders to integrate and serve their hardware. The expansion is already being adopted by Alice & Bob , IBM , IQM , Pasqal , Quantinuum and MQSC and supports the widely used QRMI and QDMI interfaces. Read All NVIDIA Announcements From SC26 Beating the Bottleneck Until now, integrating a QPU into a supercomputing center meant a new software challenge for every new QPU or supercomputing center. By building on existing quantum-HPC interfaces such as QRMI and QDMI, the Slurm expansion allows QPU builders to reuse their integrations across all their deployments. It also means that supercomputing centers can add new quantum processors to their existing scheduling and resource-management workflows without developing bespoke QPU-specific solutions. For quantum computing to advance science, it needs to be used by scientists. Now scientists can run quantum-classical applications developed with platforms such as NVIDIA CUDA-Q with Slurm coordinating access to all the…
items.title: NVIDIA Expands Slurm to Bring Quantum Computing Into Supercomputing

items.abstract: Third public-beta release of NVIDIA ALCHEMI Toolkit. The headline is distillation : teacher scoring, offline and on-policy training loops that run data-parallel, and an acceptance evaluation suite. This release also adds enhanced sampling, batched minimum-energy paths, a generative model API, L-BFGS optimizers, and LoRA fine-tuning. Distillation Train a compact student potential against a larger teacher, from a fixed dataset or from the student's own trajectories. Teacher scoring and offline labeling — a TeacherScorer protocol and public TeacherSignal specs; built-in signals ( energy , forces , stress , atomic_energies , embeddings , hessian ) are requested by name. label_dataset persists the teacher fields to a resumable Zarr store. Offline strategy — DistillationStrategy trains a student against a "teacher" ; teacher signals arrive as teacher_* batch fields, so any built-in loss term distills by pointing its target_key at one. New AtomicEnergyMatchingLoss matches per-atom energy decompositions. On-policy segment loop — the student's own propagator generates frames, TeacherLabelHook attaches teacher_* fields, and a ReplayBuffer feeds exact reference/replay mixtures. Relaxation propagators are supported via fmax and a convergence hook. Opt-in settings cap trajectory length ( max_trajectory_steps , which recycles the seed pool) and freeze diverged frames ( quarantine_diverged ). Multi-GPU on-policy — data-parallel under a DDPHook : each rank labels its own shard with its own teacher replica. Embedding, Hessian, and Boltzmann objectives — three loss terms distill what no reference dataset carries: per-atom representations, Hessian-vector products, and Boltzmann relative entropy. Evaluation and acceptance suite — evaluate_accuracy (MAE/RMSE, force cosine similarity),…

items.abstract: Announced today at SC26, NVIDIA Rubin HPC is a new GPU in the NVIDIA Vera Rubin platform designed to accelerate simulation and data processing for science, engineering and analytics workflows. As agents help scientists and engineers explore more candidate materials, molecules and designs, they rely on simulations to test those ideas and guide their next steps. Rubin HPC will accelerate those simulations, shortening the path from exploration to scientific discovery and industrial design. The Rubin HPC GPU features a record number of CUDA cores — more than 50,000 on a single GPU — as well as a sparse data acceleration capability that keeps those cores fed with data, and accelerates GPU-to-GPU connectivity with seventh-generation NVIDIA NVLink interconnect technology. Read All NVIDIA Announcements From SC26 Scientists and engineers rely on simulation to understand complex systems before committing to experiments or physical prototypes. Working with agents, these teams can explore more candidate materials, molecules and designs. This increases demand for the GPU-accelerated simulations needed to evaluate those ideas and guide next steps. “For agents tackling science and engineering, faster simulation means faster discovery,” said Ian Buck , vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing at NVIDIA. “Rubin HPC accelerates the simulations agents use to test ideas and guide their next steps, helping scientists and engineers explore more possibilities and bring breakthroughs closer.” Turning Faster Computation Into Faster Discovery Across climate models, engineering simulations, genomic analysis and financial risk, scientific computing workloads take a similar shape: an application reaches into an immense dataset, gathers a handful of scattered values, calculates…
items.title: NVIDIA Announces Rubin HPC — A New GPU to Accelerate Agents for Science, Engineering and Analytics

Quantum processors are being integrated into supercomputing centers worldwide. National programs in North America, Europe, and Asia are driving the installation of quantum processing units (QPUs) alongside high-performance computing (HPC) systems. Every supercomputer will eventually be a hybrid quantum-classical device, drawing on quantum processors to expand what’s possible in scientific research. Source

items.abstract: NVIDIA’s Ian Buck kicked off the company’s week at SC26 in Chicago on Monday with new tools for AI agents, software that can plan experiments, run code and check results on researchers’ own systems. In NVIDIA’s special address, Buck announced Nemotron for Science , the Rubin HPC GPU and an expanded Vera CPU platform for high-performance computing . He also detailed a new collaboration in quantum computing with IBM and Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory . “The frontier of computing and the new scientific stack is going to be simulation, as always, but combined with AI and the future of quantum,” said Buck, vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing at NVIDIA. Buck opened the talk by looking back to his first public talk on CUDA, at an SC06 tutorial in Tampa, Florida, 20 years ago. NVIDIA now offers more than 1,000 CUDA-X libraries , he said. Open Models for Science Agents “[Agents] have been just a game changer in how we interface with our supercomputers, with our devices, our instruments and how we can do the research,” Buck said. Simulation remains the foundation of scientific computing, “which will always be on the top,” Buck said, with AI, quantum and now agents working alongside it. Nemotron for Science combines the Nemotron 3.5 Super VL open model with a new open chemistry dataset and post-training recipes for life sciences and chemistry, Buck explained. Researchers can run it locally on a DGX Spark, a workstation or their own supercomputer. At Argonne National Laboratory, Buck said, an agent built with the toolkit took a single prompt, planned and tested hypotheses, chose which simulations to run and identified two new binding sites. “You own your data. You own the model,” Buck said. Buck highlighted other agents already in use: GROMACS: An…
items.title: Ian Buck Kicks Off NVIDIA’s Week at SC26 as Science Enters the Age of Agents

items.abstract: To train an AI model, thousands of GPUs have to work together, requiring a network that’s fast, efficient and resilient. Lambda is tackling the network piece of the puzzle with NVIDIA Photonics co-packaged optics (CPO) switches. The cloud provider is using the switches to connect NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 racks with more than 10,000 GPUs, delivering lower power, higher resiliency and longer mean time between interruptions (MTBI) to an AI factory at scale. “Networking has to keep pace with the demands of increasingly large AI clusters,” said Dave Ward, president of cloud services at Lambda. “Bringing co-packaged optics into a deployment of this scale is an important step toward building the infrastructure needed to support the next generation of AI.” Read All NVIDIA Announcements From SC26 In the company’s tests using the switches, network latency — the time needed for moving data — dropped by about 4% at rack scale and by up to about 10% at pod scale. Across rack, scalable unit and pod configurations, the network maintains the same throughput as conventional pluggable optics. Delivering Power Efficiency and Resiliency at Scale Improving power efficiency and resiliency matters because the network sits at the center of AI factory productivity. In a large training job, one interrupted link can stall thousands of GPUs. With agentic inference, one network disruption can introduce cascading latency effects on many agents. Every interruption costs time, and every watt spent on networking is a watt not available for compute. NVIDIA Photonics addresses both power efficiency and resiliency. By replacing pluggable transceivers with co-packaged optical engines on the switch package, it delivers up to 5x better power efficiency and up to 15x higher reliability than conventional pluggable…
items.title: Lambda Boosts AI Factory Resiliency and Efficiency With NVIDIA Photonics
